rv.q: His latest firecracker is unstoppably fierce, funny — and ruthless.
But above all, of course, the show works because of Jacobs-Jenkins's writing, which is probing without losing its humor and bracingly honest without being cruel.
Purpose is all the more powerful, though, for its sly, barely fictionalized reference to a specific family.
Purpose reveals itself to be something more distinctive and at times quite poignant.
“Purpose” is a brilliant and profound narrative about legacies, ambition, mental illness and who you may become if you were never allowed to know yourself.
The sheer ease of Jacobs-Jenkins's writing drives the headlong rush of the first act, but in the unbalanced second half his technique wavers.
It’s a lot — too much for one drama to hold, ultimately — but the result is nonetheless a feast of jaw-dropping tea and riveting food for thought.
Much of the nearly mathematical pleasure of watching Purpose lies in watching a top-tier craftsman set up and then launch one long domino chain of familial discord.
It’s certainly cathartic to see a work so unafraid to go big and risk bad laughs by letting serious strife spill over into farce.
Purpose vibrantly captures not just the concentric concerns of one prominent Black family, but the paradox of intimacy: that the people who know us best are also best equipped to wound us.

Yet between Jacobs-Jenkins's distinct point of view and peerless use of language, this funny, deep, and provocative work feels totally fresh.
Despite all the downed crockery, Purpose is a feast.
He secures his place as Broadway's most incisive and scathingly entertaining chronicler of family and social dysfunction
Each performance is exquisitely tuned, and though its second act spends too long on the reverberations of its perfect first, this is drama at its finest.
Act I of Purpose is sheer perfection, exquisitely and seamlessly played out in dark and darkly comic moments.
But they certainly earn a place beside the haunted Westons of August: Osage County, the previous Steppenwolf import to offer this much excitement and empathy.
Even so, it is a consistently entertaining play, and something more, a subtle, intelligent contemplation of the various ways the characters search for purpose, and how sweet it is to have one.
It’s just one of many reasons why I need, and want, to see “Purpose” again.

Simply the best new play of the season by last year's Tony Award winner.

Jacobs-Jenkins is a fantastic storyteller, and it is possible to walk away from 'Purpose' without considering any of the play's further implications, simply having relished in his almost unparalleled gifts for dialogue and characterization.
Purpose is an important deep dive into the dynamics of family, the power of forgiveness, and the need for redemption.

Purpose is less about the purpose of life and more about the purpose of family; the purpose of family, as portrayed here, is the continuity of people who know you, judge you, but, at the end of the day, love you.
Family squabble points are made, explained, and made again until we are bleary.
